Learning Objectives
Perform a comprehensive physical examination of the knee.
Diagnose knee ligament injuries.
Recognize the physical examination findings of a meniscal tear.
Recognize the physical examination findings of articular cartilage injuries, osteochondritis
dissecans, and osteoarthritis.
Recognize the physical examination findings for patellofemoral pain and patellar instability.

Often overlooked and underappreciated, a thorough patient history and physical
examination are sufficient to correctly diagnose many knee conditions. The knee
physical examination should proceed in a logical and consistent order and should
include both knees. Because normal knee ligamentous laxity varies widely among
patients, using the contralateral limb as a reference standard will ensure accurate
diagnosis of the affected extremity. Finally, the lower extremity should be considered as
a whole because the hip, ankle, and foot may contribute to what the patient perceives to
be primarily a knee problem.
Relevant Patient History
Location of the pain and any mechanical symptoms
Mechanism of injury
Chronicity of injury
Surgical history
Activity level and functional demands

Relevant Patient History
Before the physical examination is initiated, a focused patient history should be
obtained. The patient should be asked to locate the pain and describe any mechanical
symptoms. The mechanism of injury, the chronicity of symptoms, and information about
prior surgery on the affected knee also are important. Finally, the patient’s activity level
and functional demands should be ascertained because they will influence treatment
decisions.
Bilateral Knee Examination
The range of physiologic knee joint motion and laxity varies widely among individuals. A
common tool for assessing general ligamentous laxity is the Beighton score, which is easily
performed in the clinical setting. During this assessment, the patient is asked to perform five
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
2/40

joint maneuvers, each of which is graded. A total score of 5 or higher indicates general
ligamentous hypermobility (Table 1).
A false-positive result from a ligament examination is possible in a patient with physiologic
laxity if the contralateral limb is not assessed. For example, some patients will have a mildly
positive pivot shift (ie, a pivot glide) on the uninjured knee.

Examination of the Ankle, Hip, and Spine
Note the presence of pes planus and excessive femoral anteversion, both of which may
contribute to patellofemoral tracking problems.
Excessive femoral anteversion may be identified by an inward-pointing or so-called squinting
patella.
Pain felt in the knee may be referred from other locations, including the spine and the hip.
A careful patient history can help differentiate referred spinal pain from knee pain.

Routine examination of the hip and spine is recommended in evaluating a patient with knee
pain, with particular attention paid to loss of hip rotation.
Order of Physical Examination
Inspection
Gait
Limb alignment
Palpation
Range of motion
Strength and special tests

Order of Physical Examination
The knee physical examination begins with inspection and assessment of patient gait
and limb alignment. Systematic palpation of key structures of the knee and range of
motion tests are followed by strength assessment and special tests. Potentially
uncomfortable tests should be performed last because guarding will substantially
obscure the results of a ligament examination.
General Evaluation
Inspection
Visible effusion
Ecchymosis or soft-tissue swelling
Presence of any incisional or traumatic scars
Muscle atrophy

Inspection
SEND FEEDBACK

4/40

On inspection, a true knee joint effusion often is best appreciated in the suprapatellar
pouch. It should be differentiated from prepatellar bursitis, which presents as swelling
directly anterior to the patella.
Quadriceps atrophy is particularly common in patients with chronic knee conditions.
Therefore, quadriceps bulk in the affected limb should be noted, and the contour of the
vastus medialis obliquus musculature should be compared with that of the contralateral
limb. In patients with major quadriceps atrophy, thigh circumference is visibly smaller
and vastus medialis obliquus contour is more poorly defined in the affected leg than in
the contralateral limb. Conversely, patients with bilateral patellofemoral disorders
typically have bilateral quadriceps atrophy.
Gait Evaluation
This assessment can begin before the patient enters the examination room.

Gait Evaluation
To evaluate for gait abnormalities, observe the patient walking down the hallway or as
he or she enters the room. An antalgic gait can result from any condition that causes
knee pain. Dynamic thrust into varus or valgus during gait may indicate chronic collateral
ligament insufficiency (Resource 1). Finally, some patients with a knee injury will
demonstrate a quadriceps avoidance gait, bearing weight with the knee locked in
extension because of a weakened extensor mechanism or pain (Videos 1 and 2).

Standing Limb Alignment
Knee coronal and sagittal alignment

Standing Limb Alignment
During the knee examination, clinically apparent varus or valgus alignment should be
noted. Substantial primary varus or valgus deformity may be the result of single-
compartment osteoarthritis, whereas knee recurvatum when standing may indicate
ligamentous laxity. Finally, inability to fully extend the knee when standing may be
secondary to effusion or contracture.
Palpation
The knee is superficial enough to allow for localization of tenderness to specific regions or
structures. Thorough knowledge of the bony and soft-tissue anatomy is key to correctly
identifying and correlate areas of pain with pathology (Figure 1).
Intra-articular effusion
Joint line
Collateral ligaments
Pes anserine insertion
Patellar facets
Prepatellar bursa
Patellar ligament and anterior fat pad
Extensor mechanism
Distal femur and proximal tibia
Position of the anterior tibial plateau relative to the femoral condyle


Palpation
An effusion can be milked from the suprapatellar pouch with one hand while the other
hand palpates the effusion. This is best performed with the patient in the supine
position on the examination table with the knee in full extension and the quadriceps
relaxed (Figure 2).
The examiner should differentiate joint line tenderness (JLT) from distal femur or
proximal tibia tenderness. In addition, the examiner should differentiate JLT from pain
along the collateral ligaments.
The examiner should be able to localize pain on a specific aspect of the patellar ligament
(ie, proximal, midsubstance, or distal). This symptom should be differentiated from pain
provoked via palpation of the anterior fat pad.
To rule out extensor mechanism rupture in patients who are experiencing pain and are
unable to actively extend the knee, the examiner should evaluate for a palpable defect.
Patellar height in the affected limb also can be compared clinically with that in the
contralateral knee.
The lateral aspect of lateral femoral condyle may be tender after a lateral patellofemoral
dislocation episode. In addition, patients with subchondral insufficiency fractures will
report more pain with palpation directly over the involved bony area than over the
nearby joint line. This is in contrast to patients with meniscal pathology or osteoarthritis,
for whom palpation directly over the joint line is painful.
Note side-to-side differences in the position of the anterior tibial plateau relative to the
femoral condyle, particularly in evaluating for acute cruciate ligament injury or chronic
insufficiency.

9/3/26, 5:45 PM

Figure 2 Clinical photograph shows knee effusion by milking the fluid from the
suprapatellar pouch with one hand. The other hand palpates the so-called balloon of
fluid. (Reproduced from Bronstein RD, Schaffer JC: Physical examination of the knee:
Meniscus, cartilage, and patellofemoral conditions. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2017;25[5]:365-374.)
Range of Motion
Compared with the contralateral knee, the injured knee may fail to reach full passive
extension.
Limited range of motion is expected in patients with large knee effusions or pain. Although
full range of motion is required for a complete knee examination, it is not always possible at
the first visit and should not be forced.
Note knee recurvatum on standing or ability to passively hyperextend
Assess the knee for lack of flexibility

Range of Motion
A lack of passive knee extension may indicate a mechanical block or a hamstring spasm.
To differentiate the two conditions, have the patient rest the affected lower extremity for
several minutes with the foot elevated; after the hamstrings have been passively
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
10/40

stretched, determine the degree of residual extension deficit. A mechanical block from a
displaced meniscus tear, large effusion, or anterior knee cyclops lesion will persist;
similarly, a flexion contracture from pericapsular scarring will persist; however, the
hamstring spasm likely will be overcome by the passive stretch, and passive extension
should improve in this instance.
Tight quadriceps musculature is a common contributor to anterior knee pain and is best
assessed with the patient in the prone position. Conversely, hamstring tightness is a
common contributor to lower back pain and is best assessed with the patient in the
supine position and the hip flexed to 90°.
Functional Assessment
Strength tests
Core and hip stabilizers
Quadriceps strength
Hamstring strength
High-level functional testing

Functional Assessment
Many patients with chronic knee pain have poor core and hip stabilizer strength, and
their posture and pelvic tilt should be assessed while they are standing. Patients with
poor core strength often have excessive anterior pelvic tilt. Patients with poor hip
stabilizer strength will have poor control when attempting a single-leg squat, with the
knee often collapsing into valgus during the maneuver.
High-level functional testing may be performed in limited circumstances. It should not be
performed in patients in whom an acute injury or knee instability is suspected or if a
patient is unlikely to complete the test because of pain. Functional testing may be useful
to evaluate patients with chronic conditions or those in the later phases of rehabilitation
after knee surgery. For example, patients with chronic anterior knee pain often will
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
11/40

demonstrate poor hip and core strength on tasks such as the single-leg squat. After
reconstructive knee surgery, functional testing can determine if the patient has achieved
limb symmetry. Patients seeking to return to high-level activities should demonstrate
symmetric or near-symmetric performance of tasks, such as distance achieved with a
single-leg triple hop.
Disease-Specific Physical Examination and Special Tests
Knee Injuries in Children
The examination of an injured knee is more difficult in children than in adults (Resource 2).
If laxity is observed in patients with open physes, stress radiographs must be obtained to
distinguish between a ligament injury and a nondisplaced physeal fracture.
Bony and soft-tissue palpation should pinpoint the areas of tenderness and rule out possible
bony and epiphyseal plate injuries.
Discoid meniscus tears typically are present in children younger than 10 years, often with
intermittent painful episodes of dramatic popping or snapping within the knee.
Frequently, the child is unable to achieve full knee extension, and a clunk can be elicited on
examination with flexion, extension, and circumduction.
Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) in the knee typically presents as poorly localized knee pain
that worsens with activity, particularly deep flexion activities, such as stair climbing (Resources
3 and 4).
Wilson sign

Knee Injuries in Children
Pediatric patients with a knee injury often are frightened, in acute pain, and unable to
relax. The examiner should first note any joint effusion. Areas of tenderness should be
localized as specifically as possible, and any meniscal signs should be noted. Finally,
range of motion and instability should be evaluated in all planes as tolerated by the
patient. The Lachman, drawer, pivot shift, and varus/valgus stress tests should be
performed. Finally, the affected and contralateral knees should be compared to evaluate
for side-to-side differences in laxity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
12/40

In patients with a knee OCD lesion, pain typically is localized over the compartment
containing the lesion. Patients rarely report instability. Joint effusion, decreased range of
motion, and quadriceps atrophy are variably present depending on the extent and stage
of the lesion and the duration of the symptoms. Mechanical symptoms, such as catching
or locking, may occur if the fragment has become unstable or is completely detached
and acting as a loose body.
In 1967, Wilson1 observed that patients with OCD of the medial femoral condyle often
have a specific antalgic gait with external rotation of the foot (ie, Wilson sign). Wilson1
proposed that the adoption of this gait relieves pressure of the tibial spine on the medial
femoral condyle and decreases pressure over the lesion. With external rotation, a lesion
located on the medial femoral condyle does not impinge with the medial tibial eminence,
decreasing the pain associated with motion at the lesion interface. However, in a study
of 32 juvenile and adolescent patients with medial femoral OCD, Conrad and Stanitski2
found that only 24 of the patients with radiographic evidence of the condition had a
positive Wilson sign during the initial visit. Patients with a positive Wilson sign converted
to a negative Wilson sign with lesion resolution, which may be a good indicator of clinical
healing.
To evaluate for the Wilson sign, the patient is positioned supine with the knee flexed to
90° and the tibia rotated internally. Next, the knee is slowly extended. A Wilson sign is
recorded if the patient reports pain as the tibial spine abuts the OCD lesion on the
medial femoral condyle at approximately 30° of flexion. The pain is relieved as the tibia
is externally rotated, which brings the tibial spine away from the lesion (Figure 3).

J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2017;25[5]:365-374.)
Osteoarthritis
In patients with osteoarthritis, knee physical examination often reveals restricted range of
motion, crepitus, tenderness along the joint line, effusion, and some degree of varus or valgus
deformity.

Osteoarthritis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
14/40

An osteoarthritic knee with synovitis and effusion may have nonspecific tenderness
throughout the joint capsule, including the joint line. Osteoarthritis confined to one
compartment or part of one compartment may cause tenderness on palpation
maximally over that region. In more severe patients, joint subluxation may be present,
typically in the coronal plane (ie, the tibial plateau subluxated medially or laterally with
respect to the distal femur). The subluxation also may be palpable.
Articular Cartilage Defects
Even young patients with chronic articular cartilage defects may have substantial quadriceps
atrophy.
Lower extremity alignment, standing (static) and dynamic, plays an important role in decision
making with regard to the surgical management of articular cartilage defects.
Gait assessment
Knee ligament stability also must be assessed because knee preservation surgery in patients
with unrecognized instability is associated with a high risk of failure.

Articular Cartilage Defects
Unmanaged malalignment may result in failed joint preservation procedures (Resource
1). During examination of a cartilage defect, gross hip, knee, and ankle alignment should
be evaluated. After gross assessment of static alignment, dynamic alignment should be
evaluated by observing gait and range of motion. Patellofemoral alignment also should
be assessed, particularly in patients with lesions of the patellofemoral articulation. If
patellofemoral pathology is suspected, the patient should be evaluated for
patellofemoral maltracking and the J sign. In a patient with a positive J sign, the patella
exhibits exaggerated lateralization as the knee reaches near-full extension.
Any limitations in the stance phase of gait (ie, antalgic gait) should be noted (Resource
1). Any valgus or varus thrust throughout the stance phase of the gait cycle also should
be identified and investigated.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
15/40

Meniscal Tear
The classic mechanism of injury for a meniscal tear is a twisting moment through the knee in a
flexed, weight-bearing position.3
Loss of motion, particularly extension, may represent a displaced segment of meniscus.
JLT
McMurray circumduction test
Apley grind test
Thessaly test
Composite clinical examination versus MRI

Meniscal Tear
In patients with a meniscal tear, pain experienced at the time of injury varies and is
followed by the insidious onset of an effusion over the next day. A knee effusion
frequently is an important indicator of a meniscal injury and may be associated with
reduction in quadriceps strength. Patients may experience mechanical symptoms, such
as catching, locking, clicking, or instability, and usually report medial or lateral joint line
pain. If a meniscal tear is suspected, a detailed ligament examination also may detect a
concomitant ligament injury (Resource 5).
If a displaced meniscal tear is blocking knee range of motion, reduction of the displaced
fragment should be attempted. This can be done by applying a valgus force on the knee
in 10° to 30° of flexion and gradually bringing the knee into full extension. Lateral tears
are reduced via a varus force applied in 20° to 60° of knee flexion (ie, figure-of-4
position) followed by gradual extension. If the displaced fragment is successfully
reduced, then the knee is immobilized in extension until surgical management to
prevent re-displacement or additional meniscal damage. If the displaced fragment
cannot be reduced, then surgical reduction and repair is performed as soon as possible
to minimize the risk of arthrofibrosis and chondral damage.
An effusion in combination with JLT is one of the most sensitive and reliable signs of a
meniscal tear.4 In a meta-analysis of clinical tests for meniscal injury, the mean

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
16/40

sensitivity and specificity of the JTL test were 76% and 77%, respectively.4 JLT should be
differentiated from tenderness over the more distal pes anserine bursa.4
McMurray5 described a circumduction test to detect occult tears of the posterior horns
of the menisci. With the patient in the supine position, the affected knee is fully flexed,
and the examiner grasps the foot with one hand and steadies the knee with the other.
The tibia is rotated internally, and the knee is extended to test for a lateral meniscal tear
and then externally rotated and extended to test for a medial meniscal tear (Figure 4).
Anatomically, the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus is brought under the lateral
femoral condyle with flexion and internal rotation and is stressed as the knee is
extended. The medial meniscus is similarly entrapped with external rotation (Figure 5).
Although McMurray5 described a palpable click or clunk, the maneuver has been
modified so that pain along the tested joint line is considered notable. Because the test
is designed to displace an occult posterior horn tear, it may not be as useful for an
already displaced meniscal tear.
Figure 4 Clinical photographs show the McMurray circumduction examination. A, In the
lateral McMurray circumduction examination, the patient’s knee is fully flexed and the
tibia is internally rotated (white arrow), engaging the posterior horn of the lateral
meniscus under the lateral femoral condyle. The knee is then extended (black arrow),
entrapping the meniscus. B, In the medial McMurray circumduction examination, the
patient’s knee is fully flexed and the tibia is externally rotated (white arrow), engaging
the posterior horn of the medial meniscus under the medial femoral condyle. The knee
is then extended (black arrow), entrapping the meniscus. (Reproduced from Bronstein
RD, Schaffer JC: Physical examination of the knee: Meniscus, cartilage, and
patellofemoral conditions. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2017;25[5]:365-374.)

Figure 5 Photographs of a knee model show the anatomic principles of the McMurray
circumduction examination, with internal rotation of the tibia and entrapment of the
lateral meniscus (A) and external rotation of the tibia and entrapment of the medial
meniscus (B). (Reproduced from Bronstein RD, Schaffer JC: Physical examination of the

2017;25[5]:365-374.)
In a meta-analysis,4 the pooled mean sensitivity and specificity of the McMurray
circumduction test were 55% and 77%, respectively. In addition, in studies that reported
medial and lateral meniscus testing separately, the McMurray circumduction test was
associated with higher sensitivity medially but higher specificity laterally.6
As described by Apley,3 this test requires that the patient lie prone on an examination
table that is no more than 2 feet high so the examiner can place his or her knee over the
patient’s posterior thigh, stabilizing the femur. With the knee flexed 90°, the examiner
powerfully rotates the tibia externally—first neutrally loaded, next in distraction, and
then in compression. Substantially increased pain in distraction compared with the
neutral position indicates a rotational sprain, whereas increased pain during
compression indicates a meniscal tear. Similar to McMurray,5 Apley3 noted that internal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
18/40

rotation can be applied to test the lateral meniscus and a more acute knee flexion angle
can be applied to test the posterior horn. Because most clinical offices do not have an
examination table that is 2 feet high for conducting a test with substantial distraction,
the Apley grind test currently is more commonly performed with prone compression and
rotation. However, patients with patellofemoral pain often have pain with prone
compression and rotation, which can confound test results. In a meta-analysis,4 the
pooled mean sensitivity and specificity of the Apley grind test were 22% and 88%,
respectively.
The Thessaly test, named for its region of origin in Greece, was described by Karachalios
et al7 in 2005. The Thessaly test is performed with the patient standing on one foot,
which is fixed flat on the ground (ie, first the normal side for training, then the injured
side), and with the knee at a fixed angle of flexion (ie, first at 5°, then at 20°). The
examiner supports the patient by the hands, and the patient internally and externally
rotates his or her body three times. This reproduces dynamic load transmission and
stresses the meniscus. Medial or lateral joint line discomfort or popping constitutes a
positive test.
In the original article by Karachalios et al,7 the Thessaly test had very high sensitivity and
specificity; however, subsequent evaluation has demonstrated sensitivity and specificity
similar to that of the McMurray circumduction test.8 A large study of 593 patients
reported an estimated 64% sensitivity and 53% specificity for the Thessaly test.9 The
Thessaly test is less accurate in patients with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears,
demonstrating that normal biomechanics are important if provocative maneuvers are
used to assess for meniscal tears.10
The performance of multiple meniscal tests improves diagnostic accuracy.8 In addition,
clinical evaluation by an experienced examiner may be as accurate as MRI in detecting
arthroscopically confirmed meniscal lesions.11 Rayan et al12 found that composite
testing via McMurray circumduction and JLT tests had an 86% sensitivity and 73%
specificity for the diagnosis of medial meniscal tears, which was somewhat better than
that of MRI, and a 56% sensitivity and 95% specificity for the diagnosis of lateral meniscal
tears, which was comparable with that of MRI.

ACL Injury
Anterior drawer test (Resources 6 and 7; Video 3)
Lachman test
The Lachman test is graded according to the degree of anterior translation and the presence
of a soft or firm end point.
Compared with the uninjured knee
Grade 1 positive Lachman test: anterior translation of 1 to 5 mm compared with that of
the uninjured knee
Grade 2 positive Lachman test: anterior translation of 6 to 10 mm compared with that of
the uninjured knee
Grade 3 positive Lachman test: anterior translation greater than 10 mm compared with
that of the uninjured knee
Grades 1 to 3 may be assigned based on KT-1000 arthrometer measurements or may be
clinically estimated.
Further classification includes a letter grade of A for a firm or hard end point and a letter
grade of B for a soft end point.
Pivot shift test
A positive pivot shift test also can be graded.
Grade 1 is a pivot glide.
Grade 2 is a pivot clunk.
Grade 3 is a pivot lock.
Alternative tests for ACL injury
The patellofemoral joint should be carefully examined if bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft
is being considered for reconstruction.
Anterior laxity can be measured preoperatively and postoperatively with the use of an
arthrometer.
If a KT-1000 arthrometer is used, anterior translation greater than 10 mm or a side-to-side
difference exceeding 3 mm is highly suggestive of an ACL injury.
Posterior tibial slope should be evaluated radiographically in patients with chronic ACL
deficiency or in those with previous unsuccessful ACL reconstruction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:45 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001069
20/40

Video 3 Bronstein RD, Schaffer JC: Video. The Anterior Drawer Test: Demonstration in a Cadaver
Knee Using an Arthroscopic Posterolateral Portal. (Reproduced from Bronstein RD, Schaffer JC:
Physical examination of knee ligament injuries. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2017;25[4]:280-287.)

ACL Injury
Historically, the anterior drawer test has been used to diagnose ACL ruptures. The
anterior drawer test is performed with the patient in the supine position with the
involved hip flexed 45° and the knee flexed 90°. The foot is fixed to the examination
table, often by the examiner sitting on it. The examiner then applies an anterior force to
the proximal tibia, palpating the joint line for anterior translation. Increased anterior
translation indicates ACL insufficiency.
The sensitivity of the anterior drawer test is approximately 50% because the posterior
horn of the medial meniscus may act as a so-called doorstop that prevents anterior
translation, even in patients with a torn ACL (Figure 6).

on the patient’s thigh to stabilize the femur while the other hand grasps the proximal

Galway and MacIntosh14 first described the pivot shift as a clinical phenomenon that
causes instability and a physical sign that can be elicited on examination of ACL-deficient
knees. The pivot shift is characterized by anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau
(and concomitant internal rotation of the tibia) as the knee approaches full extension
and spontaneous reduction as the knee flexes to 30° to 40°. Reduction is achieved by the
pull of the iliotibial band as it passes posterior to the axis of the knee.15
The patient must be relaxed for the pivot shift test. With the patient in the supine
position, the examiner grasps the right foot and ankle under the axilla, crosses the right
forearm under the leg, and braces the hand against the left forearm, which provides
slight internal rotation to the patient’s leg (Figure 8). This technique provides a stable
base and allows the examiner to slowly flex the knee with great control. The left hand is
placed over the proximal fibula, and valgus force is applied to the knee. The valgus force
impinges the subluxated tibial plateau, preventing a too-easy reduction. As the examiner
maintains this valgus force and slight internal rotation, the knee is slowly flexed. As it
passes 30° to 40° of flexion, reduction occurs and often is identified by the patient as the
instability symptom. In patients under anesthesia, the pivot shift test has 98% specificity.

Because the pivot shift test involves applying a valgus stress to the knee, testing should
be limited in patients with a medial injury. In these patients, changes in the mechanics of
the knee with loss of the medial hinge may affect the reliability of the test; however, this
phenomenon has not been studied. Finally, the examiner must distinguish between a
true pivot shift and a reverse pivot shift, which is observed in patients with posterolateral
instability as the tibia reduces anteriorly in extension and subluxates posteriorly in
flexion.
Additional tests are available for diagnosing ACL injury. The loss-of-extension test is used
to measure a loss of maximal passive extension of the knee, which is presumed to result
from anterior subluxation of the tibia and resultant posterior capsule tightness.16 The
lever sign test, or Lelli test, is performed by placing a fist under the calf of the affected
leg, which acts as a fulcrum; a downward force is then applied to the quadriceps. Failure
of the heel to rise off the table indicates an ACL rupture.17

Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injury
In nonathletes, a commonly described mechanism of posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
injury is striking the tibia on the dashboard during a motor vehicle collision. In sports
competition, isolated PCL injuries typically occur if an athlete falls directly onto the knee
with the foot plantarflexed, allowing the tibial tuberosity to strike the ground. The injury
also may be caused by hyperflexion and hyperextension.18 Isolated PCL injuries often go
undiagnosed because the classic popping sound at the time of trauma is not as
distinctive as that associated with ACL injuries and swelling is not as severe; in addition,
recurrent instability is rare.19
The posterior sag sign may detect loss of anterior tibial step-off without any
manipulation of the joint.20 In this test, the hip is flexed to 45°, and the knee is flexed to
90°, causing loss of the normal anterior tibial step-off in patients with a PCL injury.

Typically, if the knee is flexed to 90°, the anteromedial tibial plateau extends 1 cm
anteriorly beyond the medial femoral condyle.20 In a randomized, controlled, blinded
study of chronic tears, the sensitivity and specificity of the posterior sag test were 79%
and 100%, respectively.21
The posterior drawer test essentially adds a posteriorly directed force to the posterior
sag sign. During this test, the patient’s hip is flexed to 45° and the knee is flexed to 90°.
The foot is positioned in neutral rotation (versus the slight external rotation in the
posterolateral rotary drawer test). The examiner then immobilizes the foot (often by
sitting on it), places the thumbs on the tibial plateau, and pushes posteriorly on the tibia
to assess for increased translation compared with the contralateral side (Figure 9). The
sensitivity of the posterior drawer test has been noted to be as low as 51% for the
diagnosis of acute PCL tears;22 however, the posterior drawer test has been noted to be
associated with a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 99% for the diagnosis of chronic
tears.21
The patient positioning for the quadriceps active test is the same as that for the
posterior drawer test, but the patient is asked to slightly contract the quadriceps rather
than having the examiner apply force. In a PCL-deficient knee placed in the resting 90°
flexion position, the tibia is subluxated posteriorly, but activation of the quadriceps
causes the patellar tendon to reduce the tibia. This observable reduction constitutes a
positive test. In a randomized, controlled, blinded study, Rubinstein et al21 reported that
the quadriceps active test had a sensitivity and specificity of 54% and 97%, respectively.

Symptoms suggestive of medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury are tenderness along the
MCL and maximal tenderness at the proximal insertion, mid-substance, or distal
insertion. The femoral MCL attachment is the most common site of injury and may be
focally tender to palpation. Other structures in the region of the MCL also may be
tender, such as the medial patellofemoral ligament at the medial femoral epicondyle, the
joint line at the middle of the MCL, and the pes anserine bursa at the distal MCL.
Pain or laxity with valgus stress applied through the knee indicates an MCL injury. In
addition, medial pain with valgus stress helps differentiate an MCL injury from a medial
meniscus tear, which is unloaded with valgus stress. Valgus stress tests should be
performed with the knee in full extension and 30° of flexion. If opening is detected with
the knee in full extension, injuries to the posterior oblique ligament and the posterior
capsule should be suspected. If opening is detected at 30° of flexion but not at full
extension, the MCL is injured and the posteromedial corner structures are intact. To
prevent false-positive results for physiologic opening, findings from valgus stress testing
on the affected knee should be routinely compared with those on the contralateral knee.
The anteromedial drawer test may be used to assess abnormal medial compartment
rotation and anterior translation and to help isolate the posterior oblique ligament and
the posteromedial capsule. During the test, the affected knee is flexed 90° with the foot
internally rotated and fixed at 15° as an anterior force is applied to the tibia. Asymmetric
increased translation indicates a substantial injury to these structures.

Lateral Collateral Ligament and Posterolateral Corner Injuries
In knee dislocations, acute injuries to the posterolateral corner (PLC) often accompany
cruciate ligament tears. In addition, 25% of PLC injuries are associated with peroneal
nerve injuries.23 Regardless, chronic lateral ligamentous laxity may be missed during the
evaluation of patients with knee dysfunction. Clinically, chronic PLC injuries manifest as
hyperextension and varus deformities. In patients with chronic injury, varus thrust may
be observed during gait. To diagnose lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and PLC injuries,
varus stress tests should be conducted with the knee in full extension and 30° of
extension to assess the integrity of the lateral side. Positive results for the
hyperextension recurvatum and reverse pivot shift tests also may be signs of severe or
chronic posterolateral instability.
The LCL may be directly palpated by having the patient flex the affected knee to 90° and
rest the ankle on the contralateral leg to form the figure-of-4 position. This position
places varus stress on the knee and opens the lateral joint line, allowing the examiner to
palpate the intact taut ligament. LCL sprains most commonly affect the fibular
attachment, and tenderness may localize here.
Similar to the MCL, the LCL is best isolated in 30° of flexion, and the varus stress test
should be performed in 0° and 30° of flexion. Laxity at 0° indicates more severe
pathology, including injury to the PLC and/or associated cruciate ligaments and the
LCL.24 Comparisons should always be made between the affected and contralateral legs
because some amount of physiologic gapping may be normal with varus stress results.
A varus thrust gait, in which the knee joint is subluxated in varus on foot strike, may be
readily noted on physical examination, particularly patients with chronic instability. The
examiner should be aware that some patients may have learned to compensate with a
flexed knee gait pattern or may have an underlying varus knee deformity with medial
compartment collapse rather than lateral opening, which may obscure physical
examination findings.25

The external rotation recurvatum test is the most basic special test for PLC injury. During
this maneuver, the examiner supports the relaxed lower extremity by the great toe and
assesses the position of the knee. If compared with the contralateral side, tibial external
rotation, knee varus alignment, and relative hyperextension (which can be measured
with the a goniometer or via heel-height comparison) may indicate PLC injury.26 The
sensitivity of the external rotation recurvatum test ranges from 33% to 94%.27
First described by Hughston and Norwood26 in 1980, the posterolateral rotary drawer
test is a variation of the standard posterior drawer test for PCL evaluation. With the knee
flexed to 90°, the hip flexed to 45°, and the foot fixed in slight external rotation, a
posteriorly directed force is applied through the tibial tuberosity. The PCL is relaxed in
this position, allowing rotary and translator laxity. The key point is to quantify the
amount of translation versus rotation and to compare this with the same test performed
with the knee in neutral rotation. In patients with an isolated PLC injury, more rotatory
instability will be observed with slight external rotation than with neutral rotation
because the PCL provides more translational stability with neutral rotation. In addition,
more translatory instability than rotary instability will be observed.24
During the reverse pivot shift test, the affected knee is flexed approximately 80° to 90°,
and valgus and external rotation forces are applied. The knee is then slowly extended. In
patients with a PLC injury, the tibia is posteriorly subluxated in flexion, and the iliotibial
band causes the tibia to reduce anteriorly approximately 30° to 40°. This contrasts with
the standard pivot shift test, in which the tibia is anteriorly subluxated in extension and
reduces in flexion.
The dial test can differentiate an isolated PLC injury from a combined PLC and PCL injury.
For the dial test, the patient must be in the prone position to allow for simultaneous
bilateral testing and to visually examine the posterior knee for complications, such as
ecchymosis and swelling. During the test, both knees are flexed first to 30° (which best
isolates the PLC) and then to 90°, with external rotation applied to the tibias at each
position. The feet, with the ankles fully dorsiflexed to minimize laxity, are used as a
marker for tibial rotation. At 30° of knee flexion, a 15° or greater increase in external
rotation compared with the contralateral side is indicative of a PLC injury. A positive dial
test (ie, 15° or more increased external rotation) at 30° but not at 90° indicates an

Extensor Mechanism Injuries
Quadriceps tendon tears usually occur in patients older than 40 years, whereas patellar
tendon ruptures tend to be higher energy injuries and occur in patients younger than 40
years. The mechanism of injury usually is an eccentric load, such as stepping in a hole,
missing a stair step, or jumping. Patients typically report a painful, swollen knee, a
sensation of giving way, and an inability to walk unassisted.
In patients with a history of acute injury, a quadriceps or patellar tendon tear is
diagnosed by the inability to extend the knee against gravity and a palpable defect
directly proximal or distal to the patella. In larger patients or those with major associated
soft-tissue swelling, palpation of the defect may be difficult, particularly in those with a
quadriceps tendon rupture.
If a quadriceps or patellar tendon rupture is suspected and the defect cannot be
palpated, advanced imaging studies may be helpful. Radiographs often demonstrate
substantial patella alta or baja relative to the contralateral limb. Ultrasonography or MRI
is not necessary to confirm a diagnosis of extensor mechanism injury if physical

Patellofemoral Pain
Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) broadly refers to pain associated with
patellofemoral articulation. The symptoms of PFPS often are exacerbated by prolonged
sitting (ie, the so-called movie sign) or by ascending or descending stairs or other activity.
No highly reliable physical examination tests for PFPS exist, and recent test validation
studies have been limited by lack of a consistent reference standard. According to Cook
et al,29 patellofemoral pain remains a multifactorial and nebulous pathology that may be
a diagnosis of exclusion.
In patients with patellofemoral pain, the margins of the patellar facets and the anterior
fat pad often are tender on palpation. Anterior fat pad pain should be distinguished
from pain isolated to the patellar tendon.
Compression tests can be quite painful, and gentle pressure is recommended if
performing these maneuvers. Excessive force can produce a false-positive result and
cause undue discomfort to patients with PFPS.
During the patellofemoral grind test, the examiner places his or her fingers over the
patient’s patella and exerts pressure through the structure medially and laterally,

Patellar Instability
Patients with true patellar instability report patellar dislocation requiring reduction or
lateral subluxation with spontaneous reduction. The etiology of patellar instability is
multifactorial and includes the bony structure of the patella and the femoral trochlea;

integrity and/or laxity of the surrounding tissues, including the medial patellofemoral
ligament; muscle tone and balance; and overall limb alignment.34
The quadriceps angle, or Q angle, is a measure of the direction of pull of the quadriceps
relative to the line of action of the patella; this angle is theoretically important because it
relates to the lateral displacement force on the patella. The Q angle is defined as the
acute angle formed by lines drawn from the anterior superior iliac spine to the center of
the reduced patella and from the center of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. A Q angle
greater than 20° degrees often is cited as abnormal, as recommended by Insall et al.35
The physiologic Q angle can be increased via excessive femoral anteversion and via pes
planus through tibial external rotation.
The J sign is an indication of pathologic patellar tracking and refers to the inverted “J”
course of the patella as it subluxates laterally in full extension and then reduces into the
femoral trochlea in early flexion (Figure 10). The clinical validity of the J sign has been
questioned, and a study found the subjective J sign did not correlate with lateral patellar
subluxation.36 The J sign has moderate interobserver reliability (k = 0.53) and poor
intraobserver reliability (k = 0.28).32
In 1937, Fairbank37 described a test for suspected recurrent patellar dislocation based
on his observation that patients with this condition had marked apprehension if the
patella was pushed laterally. The Fairbank apprehension test is considered positive only
if the patient expresses apprehension or a feeling of instability, rather than pain. A
positive Fairbank apprehension test is strongly suggestive of symptomatic patellar
instability. The specificity of the test is moderately good (ie, 70% to 92%);29 however, the
sensitivity of the test is low (ie, <37%),29 with little to no interobserver reliability.33
Patellar apprehension in greater degrees of knee flexion may correlate with higher rates
of patellar alta and trochlear dysplsia.38
